findings.title: Save-then-enqueue ordering creates orphaned PENDING rows on enqueue failure (silent message loss)
findings.description: Decision 11 + 'How it works' section 3 specifies the order: `rawUpdateRepository.save(...)` SUCCEEDS, then `Mono.fromCallable(() -> BackgroundJob.enqueue(...))`. If the JobRunr enqueue throws (transient Mongo error against the `jobrunr_jobs` collection, network blip on the sync MongoClient, JobRunr storage temporarily wedged), the spec correctly propagates the 5xx to Telegram so the response is not silently swallowed. However, the raw_update document is ALREADY persisted with `processingStatus=PENDING`. Telegram retries with the same `update_id` → `rawUpdateRepository.save(...)` now throws `DuplicateKeyException` (Decision 4) → controller returns 200 OK silently and does NOT enqueue. Net effect: a PENDING row sits in Mongo forever with no worker ever processing it; the update is silently dropped; no event ever written; `ownerChatId` never populated; the `/start` is invisible. The TTL+partial-filter on `processingStatus IN (pending, done)` (Decision 8) compounds the issue — after 90 days the orphan is auto-purged, erasing forensic evidence. This is the canonical 'lost-update bug' for inbound webhooks and a real correctness gap, not merely theoretical.
findings.location: Section: Architecture › How it works › Inbound HTTP path steps 3.d–3.e + Decision 4 + Decision 11
findings.impact: Silent loss of inbound Telegram updates whenever the JobRunr enqueue fails between the raw_update save and the enqueue call. No retry recovery — Telegram's redelivery hits the duplicate-key short-circuit and is treated as 'already processed'. Affects all webhook traffic during transient JobRunr/Mongo issues; failures are invisible (no event, no log line tied to a missing update, no alarm). Compounded by the partial-filter TTL: forensic trail evaporates after 90 days.
findings.recommendation: Two viable fixes — pick one: (a) Reverse the ordering: enqueue FIRST against a deterministic job id derived from `(projectId, updateId)` (use JobRunr's `JobBuilder.withId(deterministicUuid)` or `Jobs.create(...).withId(...)` API), THEN save raw_update. JobRunr's idempotent `enqueueWithId` makes the enqueue itself idempotent on retry. (b) Keep current ordering but add a recovery sweep: after catching `DuplicateKeyException`, re-load the existing raw_update; if `processingStatus=PENDING` AND `createdAt < now - threshold (e.g. 60s)`, re-enqueue the job before returning 200. (c) Cheapest immediate mitigation: add a recurring `@Recurring` JobRunr cron `OrphanedPendingUpdatesJob` that scans `raw_updates.find({processingStatus:'pending', createdAt:{$lt: now-5min}}).limit(100)` and re-enqueues. Document the recovery semantics in the staging-smoke runbook. Whichever option is chosen, add an integration test that simulates enqueue-failure-then-redelivery and asserts the update is eventually processed (event written, status=done).
findings.cwe: CWE-754 (Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions)

findings.title: `Content-Length`-only payload cap bypassable via chunked transfer encoding or omitted header
findings.description: Decision 13 specifies `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter` checks `request.getHeaders().getContentLength() > 1_048_576`. `HttpHeaders.getContentLength()` returns `-1` when the `Content-Length` header is absent (which is the case for `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` requests) — `-1 > 1_048_576` is `false`, so the filter is bypassed and an arbitrarily large payload streams through. An attacker can: (1) Send `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` without `Content-Length` → bypass. (2) Send a deliberately-low `Content-Length: 100` but follow with a multi-MB chunked body — depending on Netty config, either the framework rejects the framing or the controller reads the spoofed length and the rest of the bytes consume buffer. (3) Simply omit `Content-Length` entirely on a streamed POST. Telegram itself sends well-formed requests with `Content-Length`, but anonymous attackers POSTing to a public webhook URL can craft anything. The 1 MB cap is the only DoS defense for `/webhooks/telegram/**` (CSRF disabled, permitAll, no auth before the secret check which itself reads the body). Without it, attacker can exhaust Netty buffers / heap / boundedElastic threads.
findings.location: Section: Architecture › How it works › Step 1 + Decision 13 + Risk R9
findings.impact: Denial-of-service against the webhook endpoint. Attacker POSTs unlimited-size chunked bodies; each consumes memory and a boundedElastic thread for the duration of the reactive save chain. With 100 concurrent attackers and 100 MB bodies each, the JVM heap and Netty direct-buffer pool are exhausted. The endpoint is publicly reachable (HTTPS-only but no auth gate before body read), so the attack requires only `curl`.
findings.recommendation: Three layers of defense: (1) In `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter`, also reject requests where `Content-Length` is missing/-1 AND `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` is present: explicitly require an honest `Content-Length` header on this endpoint (Telegram supplies it). Reject with 411 Length Required or 413 if absent. (2) Stream-count actual bytes via `request.getBody().reduce(0L, (count, dataBuffer) -> count + dataBuffer.readableByteCount())` with short-circuit at 1 MB — guards against spoofed `Content-Length: 100` with megabytes of body. (3) Set `spring.codec.max-in-memory-size=1MB` PER ROUTE for `/webhooks/telegram/**` via a `CodecConfigurer` customization (NOT global — preserves the 256 KB DoS defense on `/api/**` per user-spec line 63). Add an integration test that explicitly POSTs with chunked encoding and no `Content-Length` to assert 413 (or 411) is returned. Update R9 mitigation to mention chunked-encoding bypass explicitly.
findings.cwe: CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling)

findings.title: 401 (invalid secret) vs 404 (unknown project) status divergence enables project-id enumeration
findings.description: User-spec line 132 and patterns.md line 79 explicitly mandate 'anti-enumeration uniform 404' so attackers cannot distinguish 'project does not exist' from 'project exists but you do not own it'. The tech-spec follows this for missing/soft-deleted/malformed projectId (all → 404). BUT it intentionally returns 401 for the SECRET MISMATCH case (Decision 3, AC2). This creates a side-channel: an attacker probing `POST /webhooks/telegram/{candidateProjectId}` with a junk `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: x` distinguishes the two cases by status code — 401 means 'project exists AND has a CONNECTED bot', 404 means 'no such project'. ObjectIds are 24-hex chars but Mongo ObjectIds have predictable structure (timestamp prefix + machine id + counter) so the search space is reduced significantly for an attacker who knows roughly when projects were created. Once an attacker enumerates a valid `projectId`, they have not gained the secret — but they have learned a target for: (a) social-engineering the operator to leak the secret, (b) future attack if the secret leaks via another channel, (c) `ownerChatId` race attack (R2) timing — they know when a fresh bot has been connected.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 3 + Acceptance Criteria AC2 (401) vs AC3 (404)
findings.impact: Project-id enumeration via timing-of-creation guessing + status-code side channel. While not directly a credential disclosure, it weakens defense-in-depth: combined with the accepted ownerChatId race (R2) and any future secret-leak vector, the attacker has a list of valid targets to act on instantly rather than discovering them at attack time. Conflicts with the platform's own anti-enumeration invariant stated in patterns.md line 79.
findings.recommendation: Collapse 401 → 404 for all webhook rejection paths. Three options: (a) Return uniform 404 (empty body) for missing project, missing bot, soft-deleted project, AND invalid secret. Telegram-side semantics are unaffected: Telegram only cares about non-2xx vs 2xx for retry purposes; both 401 and 404 are non-retryable to Telegram. (b) Return uniform 401 with no body for ALL rejection cases — also acceptable, just pick one and stick with it. (c) If 401 must be preserved for ops debuggability, add a constant-time delay on the 401 path AND randomize the body/header response to remove a length side channel — but this is more complex than just unifying the code. Recommend option (a): uniform 404 matches the platform's existing anti-enumeration pattern. Update AC2 and AC3 to read 'all rejection paths return 404 empty body; only the invalid_secret counter distinguishes internally'. The Micrometer counter `telegram_webhook_rejected_total{reason=invalid_secret|project_not_found|...}` still discriminates internally for operator metrics, but external responses are uniform.

findings.title: Path matcher `/webhooks/telegram/**` is too broad — opens any future sub-path to unauthenticated + CSRF-disabled access
findings.description: Decision (Modify SecurityConfig) and Decision 13 use `/webhooks/telegram/**` (double-star, multi-segment) for both `permitAll`, scoped CSRF disable, and `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter` matching. The actual designed endpoint is exactly `POST /webhooks/telegram/{projectId}` — one path segment. The `**` wildcard means ANY future route added under that prefix — `/webhooks/telegram/admin/reset`, `/webhooks/telegram/debug/inspect`, `/webhooks/telegram/legacy/v0/...` — automatically inherits `permitAll` + CSRF-disabled. Future-Claude or a future-developer adding such a route would not realize the route is publicly reachable. This is a classic 'overbroad allowlist' issue: the matcher should describe exactly the surface that is intentionally public, no more.
findings.impact: Future regression risk: any sub-path added under `/webhooks/telegram/` becomes publicly accessible with CSRF disabled without explicit security review. Combined with the payload-size filter also matching `/**`, future sub-paths inherit the relaxed body-size cap. This is a latent vulnerability — not exploitable today, but creates a foot-gun for the next epic.
findings.recommendation: Change all three matchers from `/webhooks/telegram/**` to `/webhooks/telegram/*` (single segment): (1) `pathMatchers('/webhooks/telegram/*').permitAll()`, (2) `NegatedServerWebExchangeMatcher(new PathPatternParserServerWebExchangeMatcher('/webhooks/telegram/*'))` for CSRF, (3) `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter` matches `/webhooks/telegram/*`. Add an integration test: `POST /webhooks/telegram/anything/sub/path` returns 401 (auth required, falls through to the catch-all `anyExchange().authenticated()`). Update Decision 13 to document the scoping intent: 'exactly one path segment matches the projectId — no nested routes are public'.
findings.cwe: CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource)

findings.title: `projectId` Micrometer label has unbounded cardinality on `received_total` — metrics-backend DoS risk
findings.description: Decision 10 specifies `telegram_webhook_received_total{projectId}` — the projectId is included as a Micrometer label. Per AC16 this counter is incremented on successful (200) webhook reception, so the `projectId` set is bounded by 'active projects with CONNECTED bots'. That is acceptable cardinality TODAY (single-digit projects) but grows linearly with platform adoption. The user-spec already notes 'Telegram retries when our 200 lands past its per-update timeout' which means each project produces many `received` events. More dangerous: if the label is also (or accidentally) used on the `rejected_total{reason=project_not_found}` path, attacker probing random projectIds (see enumeration finding above) creates UNBOUNDED unique label values — each probe is a brand-new time-series in Prometheus/OTel backend. Modern metrics backends (Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics) start to degrade at 1M+ time-series; an attacker can manufacture that in minutes. Even without the rejection-path issue, the spec lacks explicit cardinality guardrails.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 10 + Acceptance Criteria AC16
findings.impact: Metrics-backend resource exhaustion when projectId cardinality grows or when attacker-controlled paths inherit the label. Each unique projectId creates a permanent time-series in Prometheus (or whichever exporter Epic 09 adds). Memory cost grows linearly; queries slow down; high-cardinality alerts in monitoring fire. For the project-not-found path specifically: an attacker can manufacture millions of unique projectId labels via random-ObjectId probes, achieving denial-of-service against the metrics pipeline.
findings.recommendation: Two corrections: (1) Explicitly state in Decision 10 that `projectId` label is ONLY applied to the success path (`received_total`) where cardinality = N projects, NOT to any `rejected_total` path. Update tech-spec to list rejection labels: `rejected_total{reason=invalid_secret|project_not_found|duplicate|payload_too_large}` — no projectId label, exactly as currently spec'd, but add an explicit note. (2) Add a guardrail: if `received_total` labels grow past N (say 1000 distinct projectIds), aggregate into a sampled `received_total{projectIdBucket=<sha256(projectId)%100>}` form. Document the cardinality budget. (3) Add a test that probes 10 different unknown projectIds and asserts only 1 time-series exists on `rejected_total{reason=project_not_found}` (no projectId tag).
findings.cwe: CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling)

findings.title: `raw_updates.processingError = ex.getMessage()` may capture user-controlled payload data + tokens
findings.description: Decision 9 + the worker pseudocode in step 3 'on exception: catch in worker, write `processingStatus=failed` + `processingError=ex.getMessage()`'. Exception messages frequently contain echo of input data — examples: (a) `JsonMappingException` includes the offending JSON token's content and path, (b) `MongoQueryException` may include query bson with filter values, (c) Telegram API errors echoed back through a downstream call could include the bot token or chat metadata, (d) a Jackson parse error against an attacker-crafted payload echoes the malformed bytes. Once stored to Mongo `raw_updates.processingError`, this string is (i) visible to anyone with `mongosh` access (developers, operators, future admin dashboard), (ii) included in any Mongo backup, (iii) potentially echoed to logs when an operator inspects a failed row. The tech-spec already mandates `TelegramApiClient.scrubTokens(...)` for log sites (R4, AC18) — but `processingError` is a DB column, not a log site, and the spec does not require scrubbing there.
findings.location: Section: Architecture › How it works › Worker path › Step 3 + Decision 9 + Data Models › RawUpdate.processingError
findings.impact: Data exfiltration via failure path. Attacker who can trigger a parse error with crafted payload (e.g., malformed JSON with embedded token-shaped string, or a deliberately-mistyped field) can plant their content into `raw_updates.processingError`. If the operator's bot token ever appears in any throw-path message (e.g., downstream WebClient error message during a future Epic 06 integration), the token lands in plaintext in the audit collection. Backup leak exposes accumulated error messages.
findings.recommendation: Three changes: (1) Apply `TelegramApiClient.scrubTokens(...)` to `processingError` before writing — same regex as the log scrubber. Add a unit test: worker catches an exception with message containing a Telegram-token-shaped string → `raw_updates.processingError` contains `[REDACTED_TOKEN]`. (2) Truncate `processingError` to a hard cap (e.g., 500 chars) before persisting, to bound the exfiltration surface even if scrubbing misses a pattern. (3) Store ONLY the exception class name + a short safe summary, never the raw `ex.getMessage()`. Schema: change `processingError` to `processingErrorClass: String` + `processingErrorSummary: String` (truncated, scrubbed). Update Decision 9 and the AC14 test to verify scrubbing applies.
findings.cwe: CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information)

findings.title: Token-scrubber per-log-site enumeration is not exhaustive in tech-spec — risk of missed site at implementation
findings.description: User-spec R4 + AC18 + tech-spec section 'Cascade order' line 79 state 'All log sites that emit `payload`-derived strings → wrap through `TelegramApiClient.scrubTokens(...)`'. The TelegramSender precedent in patterns.md line 122 explicitly enumerates 7 required scrubber sites for the SEND path (`map4xx`, `ok=false` mapper, 5xx retry observer, 429-wait, terminal failure, overall timeout, transport error). The 08-webhook-ingestion tech-spec does NOT enumerate the corresponding sites for the WEBHOOK path. Worker has at minimum: (a) successful processing log, (b) exception-catch log, (c) `processingStatus=failed` log, (d) ownerChatId-populate log, (e) per-branch entry log (`/start`/`/stop`/group/plain text/etc.), (f) JobRunr retry observer log. Controller has: (a) 200 success log, (b) 401 reject log, (c) 404 reject log, (d) 413 reject log, (e) DuplicateKey silent-200 log, (f) enqueue failure log. The spec asserts AC18 tests are 'split per call site, no combined assertion' (matches `BotControllerIT.java:399` precedent) — but without an exhaustive list, the implementing task may miss a site, and the test author won't know it was missed.
findings.location: Section: Architecture › How it works › step 4 + Acceptance Criteria AC18 + Risks R4
findings.impact: Token leak in production logs at a site the spec failed to enumerate. Bot token is high-value (full control of the bot — send/receive messages, change webhook, leak subscribers). One missed log site that emits payload-derived content with a user-injected token-shaped string defeats the entire scrubber strategy. The pattern document explicitly cites this risk for SEND path; webhook path inherits the same risk surface.
findings.recommendation: Update tech-spec Architecture › How it works step 4 to enumerate every log site (controller-side and worker-side) that emits payload-derived content. Mirror patterns.md line 122 format. Each enumerated site gets its own per-site `ListAppender<ILoggingEvent>` test in `TelegramWebhookControllerIT` and `ProcessTelegramUpdateJobTest` filtered by `Logger.getName()` + `Level`. Add an Acceptance Criterion: 'Every `log.warn`/`log.error`/`log.info` call inside `webhook/` package that takes a String argument derived from `RawUpdate.payload` or `TelegramUpdate` is wrapped in `scrubTokens(...)` — verified by grep `grep -rn 'log\.' backend/src/main/java/com/botfunnel/webhook/` and inspection of each match'.
findings.cwe: CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)

findings.title: `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter` does not increment the rejection counter — observability gap on the DoS-defense path
findings.description: Decision 10 lists `telegram_webhook_rejected_total{reason=...|payload_too_large}` as one of the four counters. Decision 13 designs `WebhookPayloadSizeFilter` to short-circuit with 413 BEFORE the security filter chain and BEFORE the controller. The filter is a `WebFilter`, not a controller method. Per Decision 13: 'short-circuit with `response.setStatusCode(PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE)` + complete chain'. There is no design instruction to inject `MeterRegistry` into the filter and tick the counter. Result: the `payload_too_large` reason will read zero in production unless the controller is the one tracking it (it isn't — it never sees the request). This means a DoS attack with oversized payloads is invisible on the operator's dashboard. The very reason this counter exists per AC16 — 'rejection-причины (controller-сторона)' — is the side that doesn't see the rejection.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 10 + Decision 13 + Acceptance Criteria AC16 (rejected_total reasons)
findings.impact: DoS-detection blind spot. Operators looking at the `telegram_webhook_rejected_total{reason=payload_too_large}` time-series in monitoring will see flatline zeros even during an active DoS-by-oversized-payload attack, because the filter that performs the rejection does not increment the counter. Mean time to detect the attack is correspondingly higher.
findings.recommendation: Update Decision 13: 'WebhookPayloadSizeFilter is `@Component` and injects `MeterRegistry`. On rejection path, increment `telegram_webhook_rejected_total{reason=payload_too_large}` before short-circuiting. Add the corresponding AC16 test asserting that after a POST of 1.5 MB payload, `meterRegistry.find("telegram_webhook_rejected_total").tag("reason", "payload_too_large").counter().count() == 1`.' Also document that this is the only counter incremented by a filter rather than the controller — operator runbooks should know.

findings.title: Unsalted SHA-256 for webhook secret — defense-in-depth gap (rainbow-table risk if attacker provides chosen secrets)
findings.description: Decision 2 + patterns.md line 101 store the webhook secret as `SHA-256(secret)` in hex, no salt, no HMAC. The reasoning is sound for Telegram-generated secrets (high-entropy, ≥128 bits, infeasible to rainbow-table). However: (a) The tech-spec does not document the secret's entropy floor or whether secrets are server-generated or accepted from the operator. If the operator can ever supply a low-entropy secret (e.g., `mybotsecret123`), unsalted SHA-256 falls instantly to dictionary attack on a leaked hash. (b) Unsalted SHA-256 enables chosen-prefix collisions only theoretically here, but more importantly: an attacker with access to the hash AND ability to brute-force can pre-compute massive tables once and reuse across the platform (every bot uses the same hash function with no per-bot salt). HMAC-SHA256 with a server-side pepper, or PBKDF2/Argon2 with per-row salt, are the standard defense-in-depth. (c) The pattern is already established in `BotService.connect` — changing it requires data migration. So this is a forward-looking concern.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 2 + Decision 15 (Sha256Hex extraction) + patterns.md line 101
findings.impact: If the Mongo `bots` collection is exfiltrated (backup leak, replica compromise) AND any operator supplied a low-entropy secret, attacker can recover the plaintext secret via dictionary attack and forge inbound Telegram updates for that bot. With server-generated high-entropy secrets the impact is minimal (computationally infeasible).
findings.recommendation: Three options ordered by cost: (1) Cheapest: document an explicit minimum-entropy invariant for the secret (e.g., 'secrets are server-generated, ≥32 bytes, SecureRandom') and add a test that the Connect flow rejects operator-supplied secrets shorter than N bytes. Update Decision 2 to record this invariant. (2) Add a server-side pepper (env var `WEBHOOK_SECRET_PEPPER`) used as `SHA-256(pepper || secret)` — single new dependency on env-configured pepper, zero migration if rolled out with both-old-and-new hash columns then cutover. (3) Migrate to HMAC-SHA256(serverKey, secret) — strongest, requires data migration. For 04b: option (1) is sufficient if secrets are confirmed server-generated. Add an explicit Decision: 'Webhook secrets are generated via `SecureRandom`, base64-encoded, 32 bytes — no operator-supplied path exists.'
findings.cwe: CWE-916 (Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort)

findings.title: OwnerChatId race (R2) accepted without documented detection or rollback mechanism
findings.description: Decision 5 + Risk R2 explicitly accept the race: a fast attacker who learns `@botusername` immediately after Connect can race the owner's `/start` and capture `ownerChatId`. Mitigation is 'instruct owner to /start immediately' (staging-smoke runbook). What's missing: (a) No detection — once the wrong chatId is bound, there's no automated check or alarm. The legitimate owner clicks 'Send test message' in admin UI, the message goes to the attacker's chat (not theirs), they see 'message sent successfully' in UI but receive nothing in Telegram. Diagnosing this requires deep operator inspection. (b) No documented rollback — once `bot.ownerChatId` is set, the atomic `findAndModify` with `ownerChatId=null` predicate will NEVER fire again. Recovery requires manual `db.bots.updateOne({_id: x}, {$set: {ownerChatId: null}})` via mongosh. No admin-UI 'reset bot owner' button exists. (c) The threat is rated 'accepted' but the user-facing consequence — the attacker silently receives all `BotService.sendTestMessage` calls and any future Epic 06 broadcast targeted at the owner — is not fully spelled out in the threat model.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 5 + Risks R2 + user-spec Threat model line 123
findings.impact: Silent owner-impersonation: attacker receives the operator's 'send test message' clicks, future Epic 06 broadcasts targeted at the owner, and may infer business activity from message contents. Operator detects only by 'I clicked send but didn't receive it in Telegram'. Recovery is manual-mongosh, undocumented in 04b. The window is brief (the few seconds between Connect and owner's `/start`) but the consequence persists indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Three additions to the design: (1) Add a 'reset bot owner' admin endpoint scheduled for a follow-up epic (track as a known limitation in Decision 5). (2) Add a `bot.ownerChatId` change-event to the audit trail: when `findAndModify` populates it, write `events.bot_owner_chat_populated` with `metadata.chatId=<sha256(chatId)>` (hashed for privacy) and timestamp — operator dashboard query `db.events.find({eventType:'bot_owner_chat_populated', resourceId:botId})` reveals 'when was this set'. (3) Update R2 mitigation to explicitly list the manual recovery procedure in the staging-smoke runbook: `db.bots.updateOne({_id: ObjectId('...')}, {$set: {ownerChatId: null}})` + ask owner to /start. (4) Document in the threat model that downstream consequence is silent test-message and broadcast misrouting until manual recovery.
findings.cwe: CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization — 'Race Condition')

findings.title: Adding `micrometer-core` direct dependency without pinned version — supply-chain transitive risk
findings.description: Decision 10 + Dependencies section adds `implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-core'` without a pinned version. Spring Boot's BOM will resolve a version, which is acceptable for the immediate Spring Boot 3.x lineage, but creates two minor concerns: (a) If the project's Spring Boot version is later relaxed (e.g., dependency tree refactoring), the resolved Micrometer version drifts silently. (b) `micrometer-core` itself has minimal transitive deps but introduces a new vendor (`io.micrometer`) into the dependency tree; no entry in any project-level SBOM or supply-chain manifest. (c) The first introduction of a new vendor warrants a sanity check: are we comfortable trusting `io.micrometer:micrometer-core` (Pivotal/Spring-maintained, low-risk)?
findings.location: Section: Dependencies › New packages + Decision 10 + Implementation Tasks › Task 1
findings.impact: Low: micrometer-core is widely used, actively maintained, no known CVEs at current versions. The lack of explicit version pin means an unexpected Spring Boot upgrade could pull a compromised version (theoretical — has not occurred historically). No SBOM hygiene.
findings.recommendation: Two minor improvements: (1) Pin the version explicitly in `backend/build.gradle`: `implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-core:<version-matching-current-spring-boot>'` (resolve via `./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency micrometer-core`). This makes the version visible in code review and locks behavior across Spring Boot patch upgrades. (2) Document in tech-spec Dependencies section that the project's supply-chain policy (gitleaks pre-commit hook handles secrets but no Dependabot/Renovate is configured per current state) accepts micrometer-core as a low-risk new vendor. Note as a follow-up that Epic 10 should configure Dependabot + license-policy scanning before more deps are added.

findings.title: No webhook secret rotation story documented — in-flight requests during rotation produce hard-to-debug 401s
findings.description: The tech-spec describes the Connect-time flow (BotService.connect generates secret + hash) and the Verify flow (WebhookSecretVerifier compares hash). It does NOT describe what happens when a bot is reconnected / re-Connect with a new secret. Implicitly: `BotService.connect` overwrites `bot.webhookSecretHash` with the new hash. Telegram-side: 04a's `setWebhook(url, secret)` replaces the previous secret atomically — Telegram sends ALL subsequent updates with the new secret. In-flight requests sent by Telegram with the OLD secret between the moment our DB updates and the moment Telegram's setWebhook ack lands will fail with 401. These are real (rare) in production but invisible — operator sees a 401 with no context (Decision 3: 401 has no body). No log line distinguishes 'old secret in flight' from 'genuine attacker'. No grace period (e.g., accept both old and new for 60s). No staging-smoke step that exercises reconnect.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 2 + Risks (no R covering rotation) + staging-smoke runbook plan
findings.impact: Operator confusion during reconnect: legitimate Telegram requests appear in the rejected counter as `invalid_secret`, looking like an attack. False positives in any future security alarm tied to 401 rate. Lost updates if Telegram's in-flight retries all hit the wrong-secret window (Telegram's redelivery uses the same update_id, so once the new secret takes effect the next attempt succeeds — but each retry takes seconds, latency increases for that update).
findings.recommendation: Two changes: (1) Document the rotation semantics in tech-spec (new Decision 20 or addendum to Decision 2): 'Reconnect overwrites `bot.webhookSecretHash` atomically. In-flight Telegram updates sent with the previous secret will fail with 401 — this window is bounded by Telegram-side `setWebhook` ack latency (typically <1s). Telegram retries successfully with the new secret. The 401-rate spike during reconnect is expected and visible on the `telegram_webhook_rejected_total{reason=invalid_secret}` counter — operator runbook should correlate with reconnect timestamps before alarming.' (2) Optional: add a grace-period column `bot.previousWebhookSecretHash` populated on reconnect, cleared after 5 minutes via TTL or scheduled job; verifier accepts EITHER hash. Costlier; defer unless ops complains.
findings.cwe: CWE-294 (Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay) — informational, not direct match

findings.title: DLQ design lacks alerting: failed updates are visible only via `mongosh` until Epic 10 ships
findings.description: Decision 9 + Risk R5 + AC14 accept that JobRunr Failed-queue + `raw_updates.processingStatus=failed` is the entire DLQ surface for 04b, with operator inspection via `mongosh db.raw_updates.find({processingStatus:'failed'})`. The `telegram_worker_outcome_total{outcome=failure}` counter is incremented (Decision 10) but Epic 09 (Prometheus exporter) and Epic 10 (admin dashboard) are both downstream. In the interim — which could be weeks-to-months — failures are entirely invisible unless an operator runs the mongosh query proactively. No alerting wiring, no daily summary email, no Slack hook. A bug that causes 100% of webhook updates to fail post-deploy would be detected only by 'users complain bot doesn't respond'.
findings.location: Section: Decisions › Decision 9 + Risks R5 + Acceptance Criteria AC14
findings.impact: Mean-time-to-detect for worker failures is operator-driven, not system-driven. A regression that fails all updates in the worker (e.g., NullPointerException in a new branch) is invisible until a user complains. The `processingError` audit row exists but no human reads it. With staging-smoke runbook executed only at deploy time, post-deploy worker failures escape detection until the next manual smoke.
findings.recommendation: Minimum cost, maximum coverage: (1) Add a simple `@Scheduled(cron='0 0 * * * *')` (hourly) `WorkerFailureAlertJob` that queries `db.raw_updates.find({processingStatus:'failed', createdAt:{$gt: now - 1h}}).count()` and writes a structured log line `WARN: <count> webhook worker failures in last hour` when count > 0. Operator log aggregation (whatever it ends up being) can alarm on that line. Cheap, no Prometheus needed. (2) Document the gap explicitly in R5: 'Until Epic 09 ships Prometheus exporter, worker-failure detection MTBF is operator-driven via mongosh — accept that production bugs in the worker may go undetected for hours.'
findings.cwe: CWE-778 (Insufficient Logging) — partial match for monitoring gap
